claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is single-phase, compositionally complex, homogeneous, and contains no pre-existing local chemical order.
Elevated-temperature cyclic mechanical loading induces localized nanoscale short-range chemical order or compositional fluctuations.
The induced chemical order or compositional fluctuations preferentially form along grain boundaries and in regions of high dislocation density.
The localized ordered or compositionally fluctuating zones act as stress concentrators.
The localized zones hinder plastic deformation.
The localized zones promote premature crack initiation.
Elevated temperature enhances atomic mobility sufficiently to promote local elemental redistribution during cyclic loading.
Local elemental redistribution nucleates small chemically ordered clusters or compositional fluctuations.
Chemically ordered clusters impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion localizes stress and lowers the energy barrier for crack initiation.
The proposed ordering-mediated crack-initiation mechanism reduces overall toughness.
Relative to the as-processed baseline, elevated-temperature cyclically loaded samples will exhibit detectable nanoscale chemical ordering at grain boundaries and dislocation intersections.
Relative to the baseline, treated samples will exhibit a measurable reduction in fracture toughness.
Relative to the baseline, treated samples will shift toward brittle intergranular fracture.
Conventional alloys typically embrittle through grain-boundary segregation and distinct precipitate formation.
The proposed mechanism is distinct from conventional-alloy embrittlement through grain-boundary segregation and precipitation.
The as-processed alloy has high toughness.
At lower temperatures or under static loading, ordering-mediated embrittlement may be negligible.
The qualitative relationship between induced local order and toughness reduction is supported.
